title: The Last Shot
full_review:
"The Last Shot" (Touchstone) is a delightfully offbeat tale -- inspired by a true story -- about an FBI agent discovering the thrill of moviemaking as he attempts to uncover mob corruption in Rhode Island.

FBI Agent Joe Devine (Alec Baldwin) is at emotional rock bottom after his beloved pooch "commits suicide" by jumping into the Jacuzzi.

Reassigned by his FBI bureau chief brother Jack (Ray Liotta) to Rhode Island, where he hopes to uncover a John Gotti mob link to the Teamsters, Joe concocts a scheme whereby he impersonates a movie producer about to start production there, as he knows the mob will be involved in the trucks hired for the production.

He hooks up with a down-and-out would-be movie director/screenwriter, Steven Schats (Matthew Broderick), who lives a depressing existence with his girlfriend (Calista Flockhart) over an unbearably noisy kennel, and offers him the chance of a lifetime: to direct the long-gestating script Steven wrote with his brother (Tim Blake Nelson), now an embittered employee at a "Bonanza" theme park.

Though Steven is initially at a loss to understand how he'll film his story -- improbably titled and set in "Arizona" -- in the distinctly un-Arizonan location of Providence (no cactus, no desert), Joe convinces him this is the chance of a lifetime.
They bring on board an egocentric English actress named Emily French (Toni Collette), and others like Pat Morita (in a cameo appearance) follow in short order, too. Joe's FBI superiors caution Joe that he's not really making a movie, but just arranging the setup to ensnare mobster Tommy Sanz (Tony Shaloub), Gotti's cousin.

But eventually, these other agents are caught up in the glamour of filmmaking, too, even to the point of contemplating a "three-picture deal."

Baldwin gives one of his very best -- and most likable, even lovable -- performances as the FBI man who gets the Hollywood bug. A bearded Broderick plays the nebbishy underdog character to a fare-thee-well. And Shaloub as the gangster with a scarred face (his wife, we learn, once set him on fire) is appropriately thuggish. The chameleonlike Collette steals every scene she's in with her nonchalant vulgarity, though moviegoers may take offense at one outrageously crude act she commits in a restaurant. Also amusing is Joan Cusack in an unbilled role.

Special mention should be made of the clever opening credits with the cast and production names on iconic movie theater objects like a popcorn container, upholstered seatbacks, the mustard on a hot dog, and so on.

Director Jeff Nathanson's script is marvelously quirky, though the jokes come in spurts, and some of them are quite subtle in their humor.

The overall theme of attempting to live out one's dreams in the face of a quite different reality, coupled with an infectious spirit of the love of movies, make this a low-key charmer, the type of film that could eventually garner cult status. Though there is some violence, the overall tone is gentle and understated.

Because of some rough language and violence, fleeting sexual activity and a crass scene of urination, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
